passage: March. Chandrika used to love her job designing book covers. Now she opened a file, stared at the blank screen for an hour and closed it. Mangoes, music, her Sunday calls with Kashish: nothing tasted of anything. Each evening she lay on the bed thinking, I'm lazy. I'm letting everyone down. It will always be like this. April. Kashish came over without calling. "You sound like a recording of yourself. Will you see someone?" Chandrika cried, then let Kashish sit beside her while she booked an appointment with a clinical psychologist. The doctor she saw later explained treatment options. June. It hadn't vanished. But one morning she finished a rough sketch before lunch. That evening Kashish brought mangoes, and Chandrika noticed, with surprise, that they tasted sweet.

qa.q: What did Chandrika design at work?
qa.a: Book covers.

qa.q: What did Chandrika believe about herself each evening in March?
qa.a: She felt guilty and hopeless, believing she was lazy, letting everyone down, and that it would always be like this.

qa.q: What was the turning point in April?
qa.a: Kashish came over and asked her to see someone, and Chandrika booked an appointment with a clinical psychologist.

qa.q: How might Kashish see the moment the mangoes tasted sweet?
qa.a: Kashish would likely see it as a sign that Chandrika's heaviness is slowly lifting with support and treatment.

grounding: It shows a young professional who loses pleasure, cannot start tasks and feels guilty, whose low mood feels permanent but begins to lift with support and treatment.

passage: "Vasudha, close the laptop for a minute. I saw you staring at that report for an hour. I know that stare. I had it at your age. I was twenty-five, new job, everything I'd wanted. And I stopped enjoying anything. Not my food, not my music, not even my niece's laugh. I would sit down to work and my hands just wouldn't start. Then I'd feel so guilty I'd sit there till midnight, getting nothing done. The worst part was the voice that said, 'This is who you are now. Forever.' It was lying. I didn't know that yet. My sister dragged me to a doctor. Then I saw a therapist every week for months, and the doctor treated me too. Slowly, colour came back. I'm not your doctor, Vasudha. But I'll help you find one, today if you like." Ganga pushed a cup of tea across the desk.

qa.q: How old was Ganga on stopping enjoying anything?
qa.a: Twenty-five, in a new job.

qa.q: What does Ganga mean by saying the voice 'was lying'?
qa.a: Ganga felt hopeless back then, sure it would last forever, but that hopeless feeling was not true; with treatment, it lifted.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Ganga's own story?
qa.a: Ganga's sister took Ganga to a doctor, and weekly therapy along with the doctor's treatment slowly brought colour back.

qa.q: How might Ganga's sister have seen Ganga back then?
qa.a: Ganga's sister likely saw that this was more than a slump and was worried enough to insist on a doctor.

grounding: An older person recalls losing pleasure and motivation with guilt at twenty-five, and how treatment from qualified clinicians lifted a low mood that felt permanent.

passage:
Supervisor's note, design team, Friday.
Tenzin, twenty-five, used to be the first to pitch ideas and stay late sketching for fun. Over the past two months that has stopped. Files sit unopened; he apologises constantly, saying, "I'm so sorry, I don't know what's wrong with me." Yesterday he told me he doesn't enjoy anything any more, not even the climbing he loved, and feels guilty for "letting everyone down."
I spoke to him privately. I said this sounded like more than a slow patch and that he wasn't letting anyone down. With his agreement, I shared the company's confidential counselling line and encouraged him to see his doctor too. He booked both today. Next: lighter deadlines for now, and a weekly check-in. — Gargi

qa.q: What hobby did Tenzin love?
qa.a: He loved climbing.

qa.q: How does Tenzin feel about not being able to start tasks?
qa.a: He feels guilty and ashamed, apologising constantly and saying he is letting everyone down.

qa.q: What steps did Gargi take to help?
qa.a: Gargi spoke privately, reassured him, shared the counselling line, encouraged a doctor's visit and lightened deadlines with weekly check-ins.

qa.q: How might Tenzin's teammates see him lately?
qa.a: They may see him as quieter and less keen, without knowing he has stopped enjoying anything and feels guilty.

grounding: Shows a young professional who stops enjoying anything, struggles to start tasks and feels guilty, and a supervisor encouraging professional help.

passage:
Thursday
Didn't open the report again. It's been on my desktop for nine days. I stare at the file and my brain just says no. Then I feel so guilty I can't sleep.
My guitar has dust on it. I used to play every night. Now nothing feels good, not music, not chai with Rhea, not even Sunday biryani.
Today was my fourth session with Dr Sharmila, the psychologist. I told her it will always be like this. She said, "That belief is part of what you're going through. It feels permanent. It isn't." I wanted to argue.
But on the way home I noticed the sky was pink and I actually thought, "Pretty." First time in weeks.
So maybe she's right.
Bidisha

qa.q: How many days has the report been on Bidisha's desktop?
qa.a: It has been on the desktop for nine days.

qa.q: How does Bidisha feel about not starting the report?
qa.a: Bidisha feels so guilty about it that sleep won't come.

qa.q: What is helping Bidisha begin to recover?
qa.a: Regular sessions with a qualified psychologist, who helps Bidisha see that the sense of permanence is not the truth.

qa.q: How might Dr Sharmila see Bidisha's belief that things will always be like this?
qa.a: She sees it as part of what Bidisha is going through, a feeling that seems permanent but isn't.

grounding: Shows a young professional who stops enjoying anything, struggles to start tasks and feels guilty, and finds that treatment from a qualified clinician can lift it.

passage:
Payal had loved her job at the cooperative bank in Satara. Now she sat at the counter and felt nothing. Her favourite music, Sunday lunches at her parents', even the new saree her husband Imran bought her, all felt grey.
At home, she stared at the washing for an hour, unable to start. Then she lay awake feeling guilty. "Imran does everything. I'm a burden," she thought. "This is just who I am now."
One morning Imran found her sitting on the kitchen floor, not crying, just blank. He sat beside her. "This isn't you being lazy. This is something that needs a doctor."
At the district hospital, the doctor listened and made a plan with her, including regular sessions with a counsellor. "What you're feeling tells you it will last forever," the doctor said. "It usually doesn't, with help." Payal held on to that sentence.

qa.q: Where did Payal work?
qa.a: At the cooperative bank in Satara.

qa.q: How did Payal feel lying awake at night?
qa.a: She felt guilty and like a burden, and hopeless, believing this was just who she was now.

qa.q: What helped Payal start moving towards feeling better?
qa.a: Imran's supportive words that it wasn't laziness, and seeing a doctor who made a treatment plan with counselling.

qa.q: How does Imran see Payal's struggle?
qa.a: He sees it as a health problem that needs a doctor, not a character flaw, and feels caring and concerned.

grounding: Payal stops enjoying anything, can't start tasks and feels guilty, and a supportive husband and qualified doctor help her see it need not be permanent.
